Every commentator begins with the same fact: the psalm is not new. Augustine states it and declines the work, having already expounded the two psalms of whose last divisions it consists, and marks the seam at the words about God's glory over all the earth. He notes that the Psalter does this elsewhere as well. Calvin says the same in a sentence: it would be superfluous to repeat what he wrote on the sources. Clarke gives the verse numbers on both sides of the join. Gill does the same, his notes here being almost entirely pointers to his exposition of the originals.

Delitzsch alone asks who did the compiling. The psalm is inscribed to David, he notes, but only because it is put together out of ancient Davidic materials, and the absence of the usual direction to the choirmaster suggests a later origin. Two Davidic pieces in the Elohimic style have been placed side by side with trifling variations, he says, not soldered together, and taken out of their original connection; and he rejects the proposal that David compiled a third song out of two of his own, calling it not conceivable. Clarke answers differently: the Hebrew and all the versions give the psalm to David, but he thinks it probable the captives in Babylon made it out of the two and applied it to their own case, praying, with their captivity nearly ended, for a restoration as ample as in David's best days.

Where the others stop, Spurgeon and Augustine work the differences. Spurgeon notes that these verses are almost verbatim from the earlier psalm, the one important alteration being the divine name at the third verse, detectable in English only by the capitals; but he locates the real difference in position, not wording. In the source these notes of praise follow prayer and grow out of it, whereas here the psalmist begins at once to sing and prays afterwards, so confidently that he seems to seize the blessing rather than entreat it. Sometimes, he says, we climb to praise by the ladder of prayer, and at other times bless God for the past in order to plead for the future. In the source, he adds, they are a song from the cave, faith beginning its battles; here they are the settled resolve of a veteran. Augustine works the smaller variations in the same spirit, explaining the change from mercy reaching to the heavens into mercy above them: it is great unto the heavens in order to be great in them. Gill records that same difference in a line, the source reading unto where this reads above. Delitzsch adds two of his own, that the repeated assurance about the fixed heart is dropped here, and that the glory which the source calls on to awake is taken up instead as a closer definition of who is to sing.

Henry alone proceeds as though nothing were borrowed, and asks how praise is to be offered. With fixedness of heart, since wandering thoughts must be gathered in and told there is work enough here for them all. With freeness of expression, the glory being the tongue, which is never more our glory than when employed on God, so that whatever gift we excel in is to be turned to that use, as David's skill in music was. With fervency, the airs lively and not dull, since warm devotions honour God. And publicly, among the people and the nations alike, since not to sing where neighbours can hear looks like being ashamed of our Master. On the mercy and truth of the fourth verse he distinguishes the two, mercy in promising and truth in performing, and observes that the heavens are vast but the mercy of God more capacious, and that we cannot see past the clouds, more of both being reserved for the world to come.
6:
Gill marks the seam here in a single line: from this verse to the end the words are taken out of the earlier psalm, and he sends the reader to his notes there. Spurgeon treats the transition as instruction rather than bare fact. Prayer now follows praise, he observes, and draws strength of faith and holy boldness from it; it is frequently best to begin worship with a hymn, bringing forth the vials full of odours after the harps have begun their sweeter sounds.

He then presses the pronouns of the sixth verse. Let my prayer avail for all the beloved ones, he writes; sometimes a nation seems to hang upon the petitions of one man, and with what ardour should such a one pour out his soul. Interceding for the Lord's beloved is easy, since the Lord's heart is already set on doing them good; yet it turns solemn work when the condition of a whole people depends on what God means to do with the man he has placed in a representative position. The petition is urgent — answer me, that the many beloved may be delivered — and it asks the right hand of God, his wisest and speediest interposition. Will he decline to use the hand of power on behalf of those whom he has set at the hand of favour? When our suit is not selfish but bound up with the cause of God, Spurgeon concludes, we may be very bold about it.

Henry arrives at the same place by another road, taking the whole second half as a lesson in how to pray. First, be public-spirited: God's beloved must be ours also, and we should reckon ourselves answered if he grants what we seek for his church even while delaying what we seek for ourselves. Save thy church, and thou answerest me; I have what I would have. Second, act faith upon the power and upon the promise — a right hand mighty to save, and a word spoken in holiness, sworn by holiness, and so beyond failure. An active faith can rejoice in what God has said before it is done, Henry remarks, for with him saying and doing are not two things, whatever they may be with us. Clarke pauses over that same clause to record a different construction: some read it as in his Holy One, referring the phrase to the prophet who foretold the captivity, its seventy years, and the deliverance that would end it.
